sections.title: What you will learn to say

blocks.text: In lesson 6 you said what people do: I work, she cooks. Now you will learn to ask questions — «do you work in a factory?», «where do you park?» —, to say «not» — «I don't gossip» — and to add usually and often.

examples.en: Do you work in a factory?
examples.translation: Is your job in a factory?
Is the salon open in the evening?
I don't talk about people behind their backs.
Where do you leave your car?
Most days, I sort my rubbish.

blocks.text: In many languages you ask a question just with your voice. In English, a question about actions starts with a small Do: Do you work in a factory? The action itself doesn't change.

examples.en: Do you work in a factory?
examples.translation: Is your job in a factory?
Is sending packages what they do?
Can I see what food you have?
Is your job at night?
Will someone look at my ticket here?

fixes.right: Do you work in a factory?

fixes.wrong: Are you work in a factory?
fixes.right: Do you work in a factory?

drill.prompt: Ask if the person works in a factory.

sections.title: Does — for he, she and one person

blocks.text: When you ask about he, she, it or one person — the barber, the fan — use Does instead of Do. The s from the action (he works) moves to does and disappears from the action: Does he work?

examples.translation: Is this where the barber works?
Is the fan broken or not?
Is chess a game he plays?
Is tennis a sport she plays?
Can you get sushi in this cafe?

drill.why: The s already moved to does, so the action has no s.

blocks.text: If the question has an action, use Do or Does: Do they fix lamps? If there is no action and you ask who or what someone is, use the clip, like in lesson 2: Are you a plumber? Don't use Do and the clip together.

examples.translation: Is fixing pipes your job?
Is fixing lamps what they do?
Is the lesson hard?
Does the animal doctor begin work early?

drill.question: You want to know if the shop fixes lamps. Which is correct?
drill.explain: There is an action (fix), so use Do.

blocks.text: To say «not» about actions, put don't before the action — with I, you, we, they. With he, she, it and one person, use doesn't, and the action loses its s again: He doesn't have a house.

examples.translation: I don't talk about people behind their backs.
I don't talk about how great I am.
I have no money.
He has no house.
The horn makes no sound.

drill.hint: One word has an extra letter. Tap it.
drill.fix: After doesn't, the action has no s: The horn doesn't work.

blocks.text: To say something isn't here, you can use There is no: There is no courier here. For more than one thing, use There are no. After no, don't use a or any.

examples.translation: The delivery person isn't here.
I can't find any tape.

examples.en: There is no bus in the morning.
examples.translation: Buses don't come in the morning.
I can't find the pliers.

examples.en: There is no guard at the gate.
examples.translation: Nobody is watching the gate.

fixes.wrong: There is no a courier here.

blocks.text: There isn't a courier here means the same — you know it from lesson 4. There is no sounds a little firmer.

sections.title: Where and when: Where do…? When does…?

blocks.text: To ask where or when, put Where or When first. Then it's like a normal question: do or does, who, action. Where do you park? When does the rink close?

examples.translation: What place is your job in?
Where do you leave your car?
What time does the ice rink close?
What time do you eat lunch?
What time of year does she pick apples?

drill.why: The rink is one thing, like he or she, so does.

sections.title: usually and often — before the action

blocks.text: usually means most of the time. often means many times. They go right before the action: I usually recycle, I often iron shirts. Not after it: I iron often shirts is wrong.

examples.translation: Most days, I sort my rubbish.
Many times, I iron shirts.
Many times, she cleans dust off the shelves.
Most days, I pull the kettle plug out.

blocks.text: usually and often don't change anything else: after she, the action still gets s — she often dusts.

drill.question: You talk about yourself. Which is correct?
drill.explain: often goes right before the action iron.

blocks.text: In a question, often stays in the same place: before the action, after who. Do you often forget the key? Does your brother often miss the bus? First Do or Does, then who, then often, then the action.

examples.en: Do you often forget the key?
examples.translation: Do you forget the key many times?

examples.en: Does your brother often miss the bus?
examples.translation: Is your brother late for the bus many times?

fixes.wrong: Do often you forget the key?
fixes.right: Do you often forget the key?

fixes.wrong: Does your brother often misses the bus?
fixes.right: Does your brother often miss the bus?
Do you work in a factory?

blocks.text: The main rule: the s goes in one place only. If there is does or doesn't, the action has no s. If there is no does, the action gets s after he and she.

Questions: Do or Does first. «Not»: don't or doesn't before the action. After does and doesn't, no s. «Not here»: There is no. Where and when: Where, When + do / does. usually and often: right before the action.

examples.translation: Are they at work on Saturday and Sunday?
Does the bus go early?
He has no house.
What time does the ice rink close?
Many times, she cleans dust off the shelves.
